primary_claim: Frontier LLMs currently fail to produce genuine steganographic chain-of-thought when solving math/maze problems under simultaneous hidden-message encoding (0/83 trials succeeded), but show nascent steganographic capability on simpler acrostic-based counting tasks, where Claude Opus 4.5 reaches 92% per-number accuracy at D=4 and 54% exact-match at D=8, with accuracy degrading sharply as digit count D increases.

effect.metric: exact match (%) / per-number accuracy (%) on acrostic counting task at varying digit-count difficulty D
effect.value: Claude Opus 4.5: EM 54% (5), Acc 92% (2) at D=4; EM 54% (5), Acc 78% (3) at D=8; EM 0%, Acc 29% (1) at D=16; EM 0%, Acc 19% (1) at D=26

contradicts_or_qualifies: Prior claims (e.g. in MONA loan-application experiment, Skaf et al.) that models 'learn steganographic encoding schemes'; the author argues these are actually dog-whistling or ciphered reasoning, not true steganography, since the encodings remain legible
Baker et al.'s reward-hacking CoT examples, which the author categorizes as gaslighting/post-hoc reasoning rather than steganography
stated_future_work: SFT fine-tuning experiments to test whether steganographic capability can be trained rather than just prompted
Further explore the boundaries of these hidden channels to ensure reliability of safety monitoring techniques
limitations_stated: Only prompted steganography was evaluated, not fine-tuning
No proof that the counting/acrostic experiment is a good approximation of the reasoning relevant to scheming or deceptive behavior in AI labs
Could not disable internal reasoning for Gemini 3 Flash/Pro even via OpenRouter prefill, limiting model coverage for the counting experiment
GPT-5.2 sometimes refuses the steganographic instruction while still partially complying, complicating interpretation of refusal behavior
quote: Current models cannot maintain reasoning accuracy under simultaneous steganographic encoding, but capabilities are improving.
